entry: French theoretical physicist and aristocrat. In his 1924 doctoral thesis he proposed that [[Electron|electrons]] and other matter have wave properties, an idea known as the de Broglie hypothesis and central to [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]]. After the wave behavior of matter was confirmed experimentally in 1927, he won the 1929 Nobel Prize in Physics. He presented a pilot-wave interpretation of wave mechanics in 1927 but abandoned it. David Bohm developed a version in 1952, and de Broglie revisited the idea in 1956 in what became the de Broglie–Bohm theory. He was the first high-level scientist to call for a multinational laboratory, a proposal that led to the founding of the European Organization for Nuclear Research ([[CERN]]). He was elected to the Académie Française in 1944.

French actor and comedian. Known for high-energy slapstick, exaggerated facial expressions and tics, he played conservative petit-bourgeois characters who fawned over authority while persecuting their subordinates. Much of his best-known work was directed by Jean Girault, including the lead in *Pouic-Pouic* (1963) and the *Gendarme de Saint-Tropez* series, in which he played the bumbling Sergeant Ludovic Cruchot. *La Grande Vadrouille* (1966) remains one of [[France|France's]] highest-grossing films. In private he was a shy, reserved man and a devout Catholic. His films drew large audiences in the French-speaking world and across much of continental Europe. In the United States his only wider exposure came with *The Mad Adventures of Rabbi Jacob* (1973), which was nominated for a Golden Globe Award. Museums devoted to him are in the Château de Clermont, near [[Nantes]], where he lived, and in Saint-Raphaël.

Frankish king and Carolingian emperor (r. 813–840). Crowned king of Aquitaine as a child in 781, he guarded the southwestern frontier, taking [[Barcelona]] from the Emirate of Córdoba in 801 after a seven-month siege. In 812 he asserted Frankish authority over the [[Basques]] south of the [[Pyrenees]]. He was the only surviving son of [[Charlemagne]] and became sole ruler on his father's death in 814. His reign began with tragedies, including the brutal treatment of his nephew Bernard of Italy, for which he performed public penance. In the 830s civil war broke out among his sons, worsened by his plans to provide for his son Charles by a second wife; he was deposed in 833 and restored in 834. Order was largely restored by the end of his reign, but three years of civil war followed his death. Historians generally compare him unfavorably with his father, though he faced different problems.

Southern U.S. state on the Gulf of Mexico, admitted in 1812 as the 18th state. Its capital is Baton Rouge and its largest city is [[New Orleans]]. Sediment from the [[Mississippi River]] formed much of its land, including deltas, marsh and swamp; over half the state is forested. France claimed the territory in 1682, and Spain governed it from 1762 to 1801, before France sold it to the United States in the [[Louisiana Purchase]] of 1803. Its counties are called parishes. Cotton and sugarcane were grown largely by enslaved Africans, and Louisiana was one of the original seven members of the [[Confederate States of America]].

Acquisition of the Louisiana territory from France by the United States in 1803. For $15 million the United States nominally acquired 828,000 sq mi (2,140,000 km²), nearly doubling the country's size. After France failed to suppress a revolt in Saint-Domingue and faced renewed war with Britain, [[Napoleon]] offered to sell. [[Thomas Jefferson]] sent James Monroe and Robert R. Livingston to buy [[New Orleans]]; they agreed to buy the entire territory when it was offered. Since France controlled little of the land, the United States effectively bought the right to obtain Indian lands by treaty or conquest.

Largest city in the U.S. state of [[Kentucky]], on the [[Ohio River]] at the Indiana state line. Founded in 1778 by George Rogers Clark and named after King [[Louis XVI]] of France, it grew around the Falls of the Ohio, the only major obstruction to river traffic. Since 2003 the city and Jefferson County have shared a consolidated government, and the 2020 census counted 782,969 residents in the consolidated area. The city hosts the Kentucky Derby, and its airport serves as a worldwide hub for UPS. Boxer [[Muhammad Ali]] was born here.

Wingless parasitic [[Insect|insect]] of the infraorder Phthiraptera, containing nearly 5,000 species. Lice are obligate parasites that live on the outside of warm-blooded hosts, including most birds and mammals. Chewing lice feed on skin and debris among hairs or feathers, while sucking lice pierce the skin and feed on blood. Usually they spend their whole lives on one host, with eggs, called nits, cemented to hairs or feathers. Nymphs molt three times before becoming adults, a process that takes about four weeks. Humans host the head louse and [[Body louse|body louse]], both subspecies of *Pediculus humanus*, and the pubic louse, *Pthirus pubis*. Lice transmit diseases such as [[Typhus]]. The body louse has the smallest genome of any known insect and has served as a model organism. The oldest known fossil lice date from the [[Cretaceous]].

National art museum in [[Paris]], housed in the Louvre Palace. Originally a medieval fortress, the palace became the primary residence of French kings under Francis I in 1546. [[Louis XIV]] chose [[Palace of Versailles|Versailles]] for his household in 1682, leaving the Louvre to display the royal collection. During the [[French Revolution]], the National Assembly decreed that it become a museum, which opened on August 10, 1793, with 537 paintings, mostly royal and confiscated church property. [[Napoleon]] expanded the collection with works seized across Europe and renamed the museum *Musée Napoléon*, though many works were later returned. The collection has eight curatorial departments and about 500,000 objects. Its best-known works include the [[Mona Lisa]] and the [[Venus de Milo]]. In 2025 it received 9.0 million visitors and is ranked the most-visited art museum.

Orbit around Earth with a period of 128 minutes or less and low eccentricity. Most artificial objects in [[Outer space|outer space]] are in low Earth orbit, peaking in number at an altitude of about 800 km (500 mi). The farthest orbits in this range reach about 2,000 km (1,200 mi), near the inner [[Van Allen radiation belt]]. Only the nine [[Apollo program|Apollo]] lunar missions from 1968 to 1972, and the Artemis II lunar flyby in 2026, have carried people beyond it. All [[Space station|space stations]] to date have operated in low Earth orbit. Circular orbits need a speed of about 7.8 km/s (28,000 km/h), and satellites below 300 km (190 mi) decay quickly from atmospheric drag. Objects in these orbits can collide with satellites, so they are carefully tracked.

Region of the atmosphere where pressure is lower than in surrounding areas. Low-pressure areas are usually associated with cloudy, windy weather and possible rain or storms, while [[High-pressure area|high-pressure areas]] bring lighter winds and clear skies. Winds circle counterclockwise around lows in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere, because of the [[Coriolis force]]. Large rotating lows are called [[Cyclone|cyclones]]. Lows form where winds aloft diverge, which lifts air from the surface; localized heating over deserts produces thermal lows, and thunderstorms over warm water can form a monsoon trough or a [[Tropical cyclone|tropical cyclone]]. Lows are most frequent over the [[Tibetan Plateau]] and in the lee of the [[Rocky Mountains]]. On English-language weather maps they are marked with the letter L.

Earliest subdivision of the Paleolithic, or [[Stone Age|Old Stone Age]]. It spans from about 3.3 million years ago, when the first stone tools appear, to about 300,000 years ago. The oldest tools, found in 2015 at Lomekwi 3 in [[Kenya]], date to as early as 3.3 million years ago. The Oldowan industry, which remained dominant for nearly a million years from about 2.5 to 1.7 million years ago, was made by early members of the genus [[Homo]], who likely lived mainly by scavenging. [[Homo erectus]] appeared by about 1.8 million years ago, moved to hunting, and spread out of Africa; it made Acheulean tools such as symmetrical handaxes. The [[Middle Paleolithic]] followed, with more advanced prepared-core technologies such as the Mousterian.

Coastal state in northwestern [[Germany]], second largest by area, with 47,614 km² (18,384 sq mi). Its capital is [[Hanover]], and it had about 8 million people in 2021. It is the only German state with both maritime and mountainous areas, including the East Frisian Islands and the Harz Mountains. The Lüneburg Heath is Germany's largest heathland, and [[Volkswagen]] is headquartered in Wolfsburg. Created on November 1, 1946, by merging the State of Hanover with Brunswick, Oldenburg and Schaumburg-Lippe, it adopted the coat of arms of the historic Kingdom of Hanover.

Chinese novelist, essayist and critic, a leading figure of modern [[Chinese literature]]. Born into a declining landlord and scholar-official family in Shaoxing, [[Zhejiang]], he enrolled at Sendai Medical College in [[Japan]] in 1904 but left medicine to pursue literature. His *Diary of a Madman* (1918), the first novel in vernacular Chinese, helped pioneer the New Culture Movement. Known for sharp satire, he wrote essays and stories such as *The True Story of Ah Q* (1921–1922). From the late 1920s he grew increasingly engaged with Marxism and leftist politics, and his relationship with the League of Left-Wing Writers was close but strained. His works were later canonized in the People's Republic of China because of [[Mao Zedong]]'s high regard for him, and critics have debated his pessimism.

Portuguese former professional footballer, a winger. He played for Sporting CP, [[Barcelona]], Real Madrid and [[Inter Milan]], and won the 2000 Ballon d'Or. He won 127 caps for Portugal, a one-time national record, and scored 32 goals. His 2000 transfer from Barcelona to Real Madrid set a world record fee of €62 million, and he was one of the few players to have played for both clubs. He helped Portugal reach the final of [[UEFA European Championship|Euro 2004]].

Portuguese poet, regarded as the greatest in the [[Portuguese language]]. His epic *Os Lusíadas* (*The Lusiads*), first published in 1572, chronicles the voyages of [[Vasco da Gama]] in a classical style akin to [[Virgil]]'s *Aeneid*. Critics have compared his verse with that of Shakespeare, Milton, Homer, Virgil and Dante. He also wrote lyric poetry, [[Sonnet|sonnets]] and comedies, and his poetry collection *The Parnasum* was lost during his lifetime. His career included military service in North Africa and voyages to India and [[Macau]]. Several cities claim to be his birthplace, and recent scholarship considers it uncertain. [[Portugal|Portugal's]] national day commemorates the day of his death.

Lightweight programming language designed mainly for embedding in applications. Its interpreter is written in ANSI [[C (programming language)|C]], and it offers a relatively simple [[API|application programming interface]] for embedding. Lua originated in 1993 at Tecgraf, a group at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro in [[Brazil]], as a language for extending software and customizing applications. Its designers stressed speed, portability and ease of use, and avoided cryptic syntax for users who were not professional programmers. It is widely used in game development, including in [[World of Warcraft]] and [[Roblox]].

Capital and largest city of [[Angola]] (pop., 2024: more than 8.8 million), on the Atlantic coast. It is Angola's chief port and its main industrial, cultural and administrative center. Founded in 1576 as São Paulo da Assunção de Loanda by [[Portugal|Portuguese]] explorer Paulo Dias de Novais, it was a center of the slave trade to [[Brazil]] until the trade was abolished in 1836. Its population grew sharply during the [[Angolan Civil War]] (1975–2002), when refugees settled in informal slums known as musseques. Industries include textiles, [[Cement|cement]], [[Cigarette|cigarettes]], beverages and plastics, and the city is an oil center with a refinery. It hosted matches of the 2010 African Cup of Nations.

Second-largest city of the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]], formerly Élisabethville, near the border with [[Zambia]]. It is the capital of Haut-Katanga Province and a hub for many of the country's largest [[Mining|mining]] companies. Its urban population was estimated at about 2,584,000 in 2021. Founded in 1910 by the Belgian government and named for Queen Elisabeth, it grew with the regional copper industry and was the second city of the Belgian Congo after Léopoldville. The colonial city center was reserved for Europeans, and in 1941 police fired on protesters during a miners' strike.

French film director, writer and producer. He has been involved in more than 50 films and is associated with the *Cinéma du look* style of the 1980s and early 1990s, which includes *Subway* (1985) and *La Femme Nikita* (1990). He co-founded the production company EuropaCorp with Pierre-Ange Le Pogam. His science fiction film *The Fifth Element* (1997) earned him a César Award for Best Director. Other films include *Léon: The Professional* (1994), *Lucy* (2014) and *Dogman* (2023).

Hellenized Syrian satirist, rhetorician and pamphleteer of the [[Roman Empire]]. Born in Samosata on the [[Euphrates]], he wrote more than eighty surviving works, all in [[Ancient Greek]], that ridiculed philosophers, priests and superstition in a tongue-in-cheek style. His *A True Story* satirizes authors of tall tales and is regarded by some as the earliest known science fiction. He invented the comic dialogue, a parody of the Socratic dialogue, and his *Dialogues of the Gods* mocks traditional stories about [[Zeus]]. His *Lover of Lies* contains the oldest known version of "The Sorcerer's Apprentice." His writings inspired [[Thomas More]]'s *Utopia*, François Rabelais, [[William Shakespeare]]'s *Timon of Athens* and [[Jonathan Swift]]'s *Gulliver's Travels*.

Italian operatic tenor, nicknamed the King of the High Cs. Known for *bel canto* roles and Puccini operas such as *La bohème*, he began his professional career in 1961. He and fellow tenors Plácido Domingo and José Carreras formed the Three Tenors, whose first [[Concert|concert]] was held during the 1990 FIFA World Cup. Their first recording became the best-selling classical album of all time. In later years he crossed over into popular music, and he sold more than 100 million records. He gave his final performance of "Nessun dorma" at the 2006 Winter Olympics in [[Turin]]. Pavarotti also supported charities for [[Refugee|refugees]] and the Red Cross, and he died of [[Pancreatic cancer|pancreatic cancer]].

Latin name, meaning light-bringer, for the morning star, the planet [[Venus]]. In the [[Vulgate]] translation of [[Isaiah]] 14:12, the term describes the downfall of a Babylonian king. Later Christian tradition applied the name to [[Satan]], the Devil, linking it with pride and rebellion against God. Some [[Satanism|Satanist]] groups venerate Lucifer as a bringer of freedom and enlightenment. Anti-masonic literature and conspiracy theories have accused Freemasons of worshipping Lucifer as a deity.

American comedian, actress and television studio executive. Her career began with modeling in 1929, followed by Broadway and films for RKO Radio Pictures. With her husband [[Desi Arnaz]], she created the sitcom *I Love Lucy* (1951–1957), which introduced techniques such as filming before a live audience. In 1962 she became the first woman to run a major television studio, Desilu Productions, which made *Mission: Impossible* and *Star Trek*. She was nominated for 13 Primetime Emmy Awards, winning five. In 1989 President [[George H. W. Bush]] posthumously awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom. After her death, the American Comedy Awards were officially renamed The Lucy in her honor.

Phenomenon or belief associated with improbable events, especially positive or negative ones. Philosophical naturalism suggests that such events may happen at any time, through natural processes or random chance, and that calling someone lucky describes an event's positivity, negativity or improbability. Supernatural interpretations treat luck as an attribute of a person or object, or as the favor of a [[Deity|deity]], and prescribe charms, [[Sacrifice|sacrifices]] or prayers. Many [[Superstition|superstitions]] are culture-specific: the number 7 is lucky in Christian-influenced cultures and 8 in Chinese-influenced ones, while 4 is considered unlucky in Chinese and Japanese culture, possibly because it sounds like the word for death. Polytheistic religions include deities of luck such as Fortuna in ancient Rome and [[Lakshmi]], whose inauspicious counterpart is Alakshmi in [[Hinduism]]. The English noun appeared in the 1480s, probably first as a gambling term.

Capital of the Indian state of [[Uttar Pradesh]] (pop., 2011: 2.8 million). The Nawabs of Awadh made it their capital, and the [[East India Company]] annexed Awadh in 1856. Lucknow was a major center of the [[Indian Rebellion of 1857]]. In 1916 [[Mahatma Gandhi]], [[Jawaharlal Nehru]] and [[Muhammad Ali Jinnah]] first met at a Congress session there, when the Lucknow Pact was signed. The city is a center of education, commerce, aerospace, information technology and the arts, and it is the headquarters of the Central Command of the Indian Army. [[UNESCO]] has designated it a City of Gastronomy.
